1-2: Trees or posts in a row: one gap fewer than the trees, and the length of the row from the gap between two.
Cutting a ribbon or sawing a log: one cut fewer than the pieces, and the time all the cuts take.
Pages read from one page to another, both ends counted.
Going up a house: one flight fewer than the floor reached, and the steps of all the flights; the task says that the ground floor is the first.
Children standing between two others in a line: how many there are, from the places of the two.
Bushes along the sides of a square, one in every corner: the corners counted once.
A child counted from the front and from the back of a queue: how many are in it.
A frog jumping along a row of stones, skipping one stone each time: the jumps to the last.
Beads on a closed necklace: as many gaps as beads.
A clock striking: the time from the first stroke to the last counted in gaps.
Children holding hands in a line: one pair of joined hands fewer than the children.
Cake layers with cream between every two: one layer of cream fewer than layers of cake.
A bus route of a few stops: one stretch fewer than the stops, and a ride counted in stretches.
3-4: Volumes standing in order on a shelf: from the first page of the first volume to the last page of the last, only the volumes between and the covers lie.
Pieces of chain joined into one long chain: one join fewer than the pieces, and opening every link of one short piece gives several joins at once.
Posts along a road, each showing how far it is to either end: the two numbers on every post add up to the length of the road.
Cups or chairs stacked one into another: the first counts whole, and each one more adds only the height of its rim.
A strip folded in half again and again: unfolded, it has one crease fewer than parts, and the parts double at every fold.
Something done a number of times from one hour to another, the first at the start and the last at the end, such as collecting the post: one gap fewer than times.
Digits used to number the pages of a book from 1: nine pages of one digit, then two digits for each page up to 99.
Square tables pushed together in a row, one seat to a side: how many people can sit around them.
A train of carriages with links between them, and the length of the whole train.
Pages numbered on both sides of the sheets: how many sheets a run of pages takes.
Two clocks striking together at different paces, strokes that fall at once heard as one: the time from the number of strokes heard.
Straight cuts across a round pancake: each new cut adds one piece more than the points where it crosses earlier cuts, so the most pieces come when no three cuts meet.
5-6: A cake or a sheet cut along lines in two directions: the pieces from the cuts.
Trees planted on a rectangular grid of rows, with a tree at every corner.
Children in a circle, numbered in turn: who stands opposite whom.
Tearing a sheet of stamps into single stamps: each tear splits one piece into two.
Strips around the panes of a window: shared sides counted once.
Lamps along a closed path put up again at a new spacing: which places keep a lamp.
Posts round a square or rectangular field, with a post at each corner.
Two paths touching at one point, like a figure eight, and posts along both.
Laps of a running track and the markers passed between two points.
A rope folded several times and cut through once: how many pieces fall apart.
How many times as high one floor is as another: the flights up to each are compared, not the floor numbers, and the task says whether the ground floor is the first.
Rings of a few colours round a sausage: cutting along each colour gives so many pieces, so cutting along all of them gives one piece more than all the rings.
A ring such as a bagel cut across in several places: as many pieces as cuts, since a ring has no ends.
Several logs sawn up: each gives one piece more than its cuts, so the logs are the pieces less the cuts.
A log held at both ends while the middle pieces fall: the two held pieces count too, so there is one cut more than the pieces that fell.
Two rows of points at the same spacing, one with ten times as many: their lengths compare as the gaps, not as the points.
A piece fallen out of a book whose first and last page numbers use the same digits: the first page is odd and the last even, which fixes them.
